list.listitem: Obstetric ultrasound should be performed for placental localization in women who present with painless vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy. B

Placenta previa (placenta covers or overlaps the cervical os) diagnosed in the second trimester should be re-evaluated at 28 weeks' gestation (alternatively at 36 weeks if asymptomatic with minor previa or 32 weeks if major previa); if placenta previa persists, another ultrasound should be performed at 36 weeks to assess for placenta accreta and guide decisions about mode of delivery. C

Digital examination should be avoided prior to ultrasound when placenta previa is suspected; while speculum examination is safe, it is generally unnecessary prior to ultrasound localization of the placenta. C

Women with placenta previa should immediately report any vaginal bleeding; controversy exists over the necessity for pelvic rest, although previa that persists into the third trimester is generally treated with pelvic rest. C

Retrospective observational studies suggest that vaginal delivery is acceptable if the placenta is more than 2 cm from the cervical os; vaginal delivery with a "double setup" (in the OR) is acceptable if the placenta is 1.1 to 2 cm from the cervical os; cesarean section is the traditional mode of delivery when placenta is 1 cm or less from cervical os. B

For women with uncomplicated placenta previa, planned cesarean section delivery is recommended at between 36+0 and 37+0 or 36+0 and 37+6 weeks of gestation, depending on the guideline followed. B The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG, 2018) also suggest delivery at 34+0 to 36+6 weeks gestation for women with placenta previa or a low‐lying placenta and a history of vaginal bleeding or other associated risk factors for preterm delivery.

For women with suspected placenta accreta, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2018) recommends planned preterm cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in place to reduce significant hemorrhagic morbidity. B Delivery is recommended between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta. A RCOG (2018) recommends planned delivery at 35+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta spectrum in the absence of risk factors for preterm delivery.

background.definition: Complete placenta previa is defined as a placenta that overlies the internal cervical os; a marginal placenta previa is diagnosed when the placental edge is within 2 cm of the internal cervical os. Placenta accreta refers to blood vessels and other parts of the placenta growing too deeply into the uterine wall preventing normal placental detachment following delivery and risking life-threatening hemorrhage.

list.listitem: 4 to 5 per 1000 births; some studies suggest a regional difference in prevalence.
The American College of Radiology guideline notes an incidence of 2.8 per 1000 singleton births and 3.9 per 1000 twin births.
443 per 1000 at 11- to 14-week ultrasound.
39 per 1000 at 20- to 24-week ultrasound.
2 per 1000 at 30- to 34-week ultrasound.
1 in 4,027 pregnancies in the 1970s increasing to 1 in 533 pregnancies (1982–2002); rate increases with increased cesarean delivery rate.

Authors of a meta-analysis of women with a prior cesarean section presenting with placenta previa found an incidence of placenta accreta of 4.1% in women with 1 prior cesarean and 13.3% in women with ≥2 previous cesarean deliveries.

Authors of a systematic review found delivery rates at <37 weeks' gestation of 26.9% for low-lying/marginal placenta and 43.5% for placenta previa, based on descriptive studies. Among comparative studies using controls, there was an increased risk for preterm delivery for women with placenta previa (risk ratio [RR] 5.32; 95% confidence interval [CI] 4.39-6.45), NICU admission (RR 4.09; 95% CI 2.80-5.97), neonatal death (RR 5.44; 95% CI 3.03-9.78), and perinatal death (RR 3.01; 95% CI 1.41-6.43).

For women with placenta previa, the risk of placenta accreta ranged from 3% for the first cesarean delivery to 61% and 67% for the fourth and fifth or greater repeat cesarean deliveries, respectively.

Based on a Swedish study of 517,874 deliveries in which women required blood transfusion, massive blood transfusion (≥10 units of red blood cells) occurred in 277 women. Women with abnormal placentation had the highest risk (OR 41; 95% CI 29-58), followed by pre-eclampsia/placental abruption (OR 4; 95% CI 2.8-5.6), and previous cesarean delivery (OR 4; 95% CI 3.1-6.0).

Previous cesarean section, cocaine use during pregnancy, previous abortion (elective termination carries a higher risk than spontaneous abortion), and smoking during pregnancy are associated with an increased risk of placenta previa.

Placenta accreta risk increases with any condition resulting in myometrial tissue damage followed by a secondary collagen repair (e.g., prior surgery or curettage, uterine artery embolization). It is also associated with pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilization, especially if the endometrial thickness is less than 7 mm.
Placenta accreta spectrum without previa was less likely with prior cesarean delivery.
Pathophysiology of placenta previa is incompletely understood.

The main cause of placenta accreta is uterine surgery. Without endometrial reepithelialization of the uterine scar area, the trophoblast and villous tissue can invade the myometrium, including its circulation, and reach the surrounding pelvic organs.

Pathologists separate placenta accreta spectrum into three categories - placenta creta (villi adhere to the myometrium without invading), placenta increta (villi invade the myometrium), and placenta percreta (villi invade the full thickness of the myometrium). Adherent and invasive placentation may coexist.

list.listitem: Screening for placenta accreta should be conducted for women with a history of previous caesarean section who have an anterior low‐lying placenta or placenta previa. B MRI may be used to complement ultrasound imaging to assess the depth and extent of myometrial invasion.

If a mid-pregnancy routine fetal anomaly scan is performed, RCOG (2018) suggest including placental localization with follow-up transvaginal ultrasound if a low-lying placenta or placenta previa is identified (and again at 36 weeks if indicated).

RCOG also recommends screening for placenta accreta for women with a history of previous caesarean section who have an anterior low‐lying placenta or placenta previa. MRI may be used to complement ultrasound imaging to assess the depth and extent of myometrial invasion.
Use of a targeted screening protocol of pregnant women with a prior cesarean section improved detection of placenta accreta spectrum and reduced postoperative hospital length of stay.
Efforts that limit use of cesarean delivery may reduce the risk of placenta previa and placenta accreta.
RCOG (2018) guidelines suggest efforts be made to prevent and treat anemia during pregnancy for women with placenta previa or low-lying placenta.
Obstetric ultrasound should be performed for placental localization in women who present with painless vaginal bleeding. B
Transvaginal ultrasound is more specific for placenta previa than transabdominal ultrasound, although transabdominal ultrasound is sufficient for the diagnosis. B

A study found that blind ultrasound sweeps and read centrally compared well with reference standard ultrasound by a diagnostic technician. This may be an option in low resource settings. Sensitivity as 76% for placenta previa or low-lying placenta.

For women with a previous caesarean section, the risk of placenta previa and placenta accreta is higher. The RCOG guideline (2018) recommends a follow-up scan for women with a history of previous caesarean section if the placenta lies anteriorly or reaches the cervical os at 20 weeks to help identify placental implantation into the caesarean section scar. B

Placenta previa diagnosed in the second trimester should be re-evaluated at 28 weeks' gestation; if placenta previa persists, another ultrasound should be performed at 36 weeks to assess for placenta accreta and guide decisions about mode of delivery. C

Digital examination should be avoided prior to ultrasound when placenta previa is suspected; while speculum examination is safe, it is generally unnecessary prior to ultrasound localization of the placenta. C

list.listitem: Patients typically present with a history of painless bleeding during the second or third trimester of pregnancy.
Is also a common incidental finding on routine obstetric ultrasound (~4% of 20- to 24-week ultrasounds).
History of previous cesarean section, previous abortion, and cocaine or cigarette use may be present.
On speculum examination, may see bleeding from the cervical os.
Digital cervical examination should be avoided prior to ultrasound localization of the placenta.

Obstetric ultrasound (US) placental localization is the test of choice; transvaginal ultrasound is more specific for placenta previa than transabdominal ultrasound. The RCOG guideline recommends a follow-up scan if the placenta lies anteriorly and reaches the cervical os at 20 weeks to help identify placental implantation into the caesarean section scar.

Transabdominal US, however, is recommended by the American College of Radiology as the initial test for women with second or third trimester bleeding or for follow-up of placenta previa diagnosed on prior US. Transvaginal US is recommended if the transabdominal US is inconclusive or the cervical os is not well visualized. Transvaginal US is contraindicated if there is an open cervix with bulging amniotic sac at or below the external os; transperineal US can be used in these cases.

Authors of a secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study found transabdominal US to be an effective screening test for second-trimester placenta previa. Using a cervix distance cutoff of 4.2 cm, the test was 93.3% sensitive and 76.7% specific for detection of placenta previa with a 99.8% negative predictive value at a screen-positive rate of 25.0%. Using a cutoff of 2.8 cm, the test was 86.7% sensitive and 90.5% specific with a 99.6% negative predictive value at a screen-positive rate of 11.4%.
Blind ultrasound sweeps performed by minimally trained personnel and then transmitted and read offsight by trained personnel had 74% sensitivity for placenta previa detection.

Follow-up ultrasound should be performed at 28 weeks' gestation; if placenta previa persists, repeat ultrasound should be performed at 36 weeks' gestation. The RCOG guideline recommends a repeat scan at 36 weeks' gestation for asymptomatic women with suspected minor previa and at 32 weeks' gestation for women suspected with major previa.

In one study of 314 women with placenta previa, identification of two of the following criteria on grayscale and color Doppler ultrasound had a sensitivity of 81.1% and specificity of 98.9% for placenta accreta, identified in 30 women:

Loss/irregularity of the retroplacental clear zone, thinning/interruption of the uterine serosa-bladder wall interface, turbulent placental lacunae with high velocity flow, myometrial thickness <1 mm, increased vascularity of the uterine serosa-bladder wall interface, loss of vascular arch parallel to the basal plate and/or irregular intra-placental vascularization. Importantly, women identified prior to delivery with a placental attachment disorder had better outcomes with respect to bleeding and hospital length of stay

The presence and increasing number of lacunae within the placenta at 15 to 20 weeks of gestation have been shown to be the most predictive ultrasonographic signs of placenta accreta, with a sensitivity of 79% and a positive predictive value of 92%.
In women with placenta previa, the vascular index can be used to accurately predicts a morbidly adherent placenta.

MRI may be usedful as an adjunctive modality as axial MRI slices can help to confirm parametrial invasion and possible ureteral involvement. In a study of 49 women with sonographically-confirmed placenta previa, MRI had high accuracy (AUROCC 0.77) in identifying invasive placenta, with 100% sensitivity and specificity for identifying placental extension to both bladder and parametrial tissues.
In one study, detection of placental protrusion on MRI was a reliable sign of cervical invasion of placenta previa.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.

Women with placental abnormalities and their partners should be counseled regarding delivery, the possible need for blood transfusion and hysterectomy, and any plans to decline blood or blood products should be discussed.

Women with placenta previa should immediately report any vaginal bleeding; controversy exists over the necessity for pelvic rest, although previa that persists into the third trimester is generally treated with pelvic rest. C

No prospective studies exist to guide the choice of mode of delivery in placenta previa; retrospective studies suggest that vaginal delivery is acceptable if the placenta is more than 2 cm from the cervical os. Vaginal delivery with a "double setup" (in the operating room) is acceptable if the placenta is 1.1 to 2 cm from the cervical os. In cases where the placenta is 1 cm or less from the cervical os, cesarean section is the traditional mode of delivery. B

For women with uncomplicated placenta previa, planned cesarean section delivery is recommended at between 36+0 and 37+0 or 36+0 and 37+6 weeks of gestation, depending on the guideline followed. B The RCOG (2018) also suggest delivery at 34+0 to 36+6 weeks gestation for women with placenta previa or a low‐lying placenta and a history of vaginal bleeding or other associated risk factors for preterm delivery.

For women with suspected placenta accreta, the ACOG (2018) recommends planned preterm cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in place to reduce significant hemorrhagic morbidity. B Delivery is recommended between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta. A RCOG (2018) recommends planned delivery at 35+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta spectrum in the absence of risk factors for preterm delivery.

Cervical cerclage may reduce delivery rates before 34 weeks and birthweight less than 2000 g. C However, the RCOG (2018) guideline notes that there is insufficient evidence of benefit for cerclage to recommend its use outside of a clinical trial.

Tocolytics can be given safely to women who present with preterm labor and placenta previa. The RCOG (2018) guideline suggests use of tocolytics for 48 hours to facilitate administration of antenatal corticosteroids based on case-control and cohort studies.
Corticosteroids should be administered to women who present between 24 to 34 weeks' gestation with preterm labor and placenta previa.
For women in late preterm with active bleeding, the Society of Maternal-Fetal Medicine recommend that delivery not be delayed for the purpose of administering antenatal corticosteroids.
Rhogam should be given to women who are Rh factor negative.

In a case series of 5 women who underwent planned cesarean delivery for placenta previa, topical application for 2 minutes of recombinant activated factor VII appeared to reduce bleeding from the placenta site without initiation of systemic coagulation.
Cervical cerclage reduces antenatal length of stay in the hospital by approximately 5 days.
Cervical cerclage may reduce delivery rates before 34 weeks and birthweight less than 2000 g, although significant methodological flaws existed in identified studies.
The RCOG (2018) guideline notes that there is insufficient evidence of benefit for cerclage to recommend its use outside of a clinical trial.
RCOG (2018) recommends use of regional anesthesia for cesarean delivery, which may be associated with lower risk of hemorrhage than general anesthesia.

ACOG and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (2018) recommend delivery at 36+0 to 37+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta previa without bleeding or other obstetric complications, and delivery between 34 and 37 weeks of gestation for stable women with vasa previa. B

For women with suspected placenta accreta, ACOG recommends planned preterm cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in place to reduce significant hemorrhagic morbidity; other approaches are discussion in this reference. Delivery is recommended between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta.

RCOG (2018) guidelines recommend planned delivery by cesarean section be considered between 36+0 and 37+0 weeks of gestation for women with uncomplicated placenta previa. RCOG (2018) also suggest delivery at 34+0 to 36+6 weeks gestation for women with placenta previa or a low‐lying placenta who have a history of vaginal bleeding or other associated risk factors for preterm delivery.

Cesarean section hysterectomy at 35+0 to 36+6 weeks of gestation is suggested for women with placenta accreta to provide the best balance between fetal maturity and the risk of unscheduled delivery. RCOG (2018) recommends planned delivery at 35+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation for stable women with placenta accreta spectrum in the absence of risk factors for preterm delivery.

Use of parallel transverse uterine incisions was reported in one case series to reduce intraoperative blood loss and improve uterine preservation. Use of parallel vertical compression sutures to compress the anterior and posterior walls of the lower uterine segment, horizontal uterine compression sutures encompassing the bleeding area (Nausicaa technique), or bilateral uterine artery ligation before placental delivery are other techniques that can control bleeding and preserve the uterus.

Hospitalization confers no advantage to patients with placenta previa who are not actively bleeding. The RCOG guideline recommends close proximity to the hospital, the constant presence of a companion, and full informed consent for women with placenta previa who remain at home in the late third trimester.
Hemodynamic instability should be aggressively managed per individual needs.
If abnormal placentation is identified prenatally, transfer to a tertiary perinatal care center should be considered to reduce maternal morbidity.
Maternal complications include antenatal hemorrhage, preterm birth, maternal anemia, increased risk of blood transfusions, hysterectomy, and sepsis.
Neonatal complications include preterm birth, small for gestational age (among multiparous women), congenital anomalies, respiratory distress syndrome, and anemia.

In cases of hemorrhage, RCOG (2018) guidelines suggest use of pharmacological measures to control hemorrhage, followed by intrauterine tamponade and/or surgical hemostatic techniques sooner rather than later.

Authors of a systematic review of 91 studies, including 6 randomized trials, evaluating uterine balloon tamponade for resolution of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) found an overall success rate was 85.9% (95% CI 83.9-87.9%). The highest success rates were observed for uterine atony (87.1%) and placenta previa (86.8%), and the lowest with placenta accreta spectrum (66.7%) and retained products of conception (76.8%).

For continued bleeding following cesarean section for placenta previa and failure to respond to uterotonics, suturing or uterine devascularization, no difference was found comparing an intrauterine double-balloon catheter tamponade to gauze packing on rate of successful hemostasis (93.1% vs 91.2%) in an open-label RCT with 204 women. The group randomized to the catheter appeared to have less blood loss.

Prophylactic internal iliac artery balloon catheterization and prophylactic temporary balloon occlusion of the abdominal aorta may reduce bleeding in women with placenta previa or placenta accreta. Negative results, however, were reported in an RCT of 40 women with no differences in PPH or maternal or neonatal morbidity.
Risks of internal iliac artery balloon catheterization include formation and rupture of pseudoaneurysms.
Fifty-two percent of women with placenta previa will experience antepartum hemorrhage. B
Nine percent will have PPH. B
52% of women with placenta previa will experience antepartum hemorrhage.
9% will have PPH.
About 0.4% of placenta previa cases will persist until term.
In one study of 100 women with vasa previa, 39% resolved during pregnancy.

In a Korean study, women with an anterior placenta previa have a higher incidence of excessive blood loss (OR 2.97; 95% CI 1.64-5.37), massive transfusion (OR 3.31; 95% CI 1.33-8.26), placental accreta (OR 2.60; 95% CI 1.40-4.83), and hysterectomy (OR 3.47; 95% CI 1.39-8.68) than those with a placenta previa in the posterior portion of the uterus.
Placenta previa diagnosed in the second trimester should be re-evaluated at 28 weeks' gestation.
If placenta previa persists, another ultrasound should be performed at 36 weeks to identify plaenta accreta and guide decisions about mode of delivery.
Some authors recommend MRI to assess for placenta accreta, especially in women who have undergone previous cesarean section and have an anterior placenta previa. C
Women with placenta previa should immediately report any vaginal bleeding.
Controversy exists over the necessity for pelvic rest, although previa that persists into the third trimester is generally treated with pelvic rest.
Discuss potential route of delivery, timing and your preferences with your healthcare team.
